titleStmt.title: A Sufficient Schedulability Test for Real-time Software Transactional Memory

analytic.title: A Sufficient Schedulability Test for Real-time Software Transactional Memory

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

abstract.div:
1
-Transactional Memory (TM) is a mechanism to control access to shared resources in memory. Though originally implemented in hardware, software implementations of TM are now available as library extensions in major programming language. Lately, variants of software transactional memory (STM) with real-time support have been presented. As real-time STM begins to be increasingly used in commercial embedded systems, a good understanding of their temporal properties for ascertaining real-time guarantees is required. Unlike the classical models of preemptive or nonpreemptive execution, in STM higher priority tasks can induce an abort cost in addition to the interference cost on preempted lower priority tasks. Due to the abort cost, several existing approaches developed for the classical model cannot be used to ascertain real-time guarantees in STM. In this paper, we convert the abort costs induced by higher priority tasks into new phantom tasks and transform the transactional execution model of STM into a pessimistic preemptive model. An existing iterative method to compute response time is then applied to determine schedulability. This approach is utilized to derive a polynomial time sufficient schedulability test for both the lazy and eager conflict detection polices of STM. Experiment results to validate the sufficient test and analyze its coverage are presented.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: In a seminal paper, Herlihy and Moss [10] proposed a hardware implementation of transactional memory as a concurrency control mechanism, which performed better than previously used methods of lock-free / wait-free retry loops [1]. Over the past several years, researchers have presented implementations of transactional memory which are either hardware or software-based. Though initially of interest only to the academic community, transactional memory is increasingly being implemented in commercial systems. An example of hardware implementation of transactional memory is the Vega 2 [21] processor. Software Transactional Memory has been implemented as language extension libraries for C/C++ offered by Intel [17] and Oracle [12].

Implementations of transactional memory with real-time support are also being actively researched. Schoeberl et al [18] have proposed the RTTM , an abstract model for implementing transactions within bounded response times in Java based multi-processor systems. Sarni et al [15] have proposed a software transactional memory library with realtime support.

Though software transactional memory systems with real-time support are being developed, ascertaining the temporal characteristics of its execution model remains challenging. This is because a transaction based execution does not fit into the classical definitions of preemptive or nonpreemptive models, which have been the primary focus area of real-time research over the past several years. Several state-of-the-art mathematical models have been developed for analysis of preemptive and non-preemptive systems, however their applicability in the STM model remains unknown. Any real-time STM implementation is required to satisfy all real-time properties most important of which is that a task should complete execution within bounded time. This bounded time is also called its deadline, and the actual time taken for the task to complete execution is its response time. A hard real-time system is said to be schedulable when all tasks in the system are guaranteed to complete execution before their deadlines for as long as the system is running.

Such guarantees can be ascertained by analyzing the response time of each task in a worst-case scenario, which is also referred to as the worst-case response time (WCRT) of the task. For the preemptive model, Liu and Layland [11] proved that the worst-case response time for a task is achieved when this task and all higher priority tasks are released at the same time (synchronous release), which is also termed as a critical instant of release. If the WCRT of all tasks is lower than their deadlines then it can be assured that the task set will be schedulable in all scenarios.

Such a test is termed as a sufficient schedulability test, since if this test is satisfied the task set is guaranteed to be schedulable. However, if this test is not satisfied then it is still possible for the task set to be schedulable. Another type of schedulability test is the necessary test. Every schedulable task set has to satisfy the necessary schedulability test. Hence, necessary schedulability tests are useful in determining unschedulability, since the unsatisfiability of this test guarantees unschedulability. Exact schedulability tests give guaranteed results on schedulability or unschedulability of a task set.

For the preemptive model an important necessary test is that the utilization ratio of the task set should be less than or equal to 1. Notable sufficient tests are the Audsley's method [3], and the closed form utilization bounds of Liu and Layland [11] and Bini and Buttazzo [7]. Note that the Audsley's method can also be used as an exact schedulability test if the worst-case release scenario is known.

Later in this paper, we demonstrate that a task set schedulable in the preemptive model can be unschedulable in STM. Hence, none of the existing sufficient and exact tests for the preemptive model can be applied to STM as they cannot provide guaranteed results. We also show that there is no notion of critical instant in STM and all combinations of release scenarios have to be analyzed to determine the response time. The release scenario leading to WCRT is unique for individual task sets and an exponential number of release scenarios have to be evaluated for each task set. This makes determining schedulability in this execution model a computationally expensive proposition.
To ascertain temporal guarantees in the STM model, new and faster schedulability tests are required.

div.head: A. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, we present a polynomial time sufficient schedulability test for the STM execution model. Our schedulability tests work for both lazy and eager [5] conflict detection policies. After introducing the basic concepts (Section 2.1) and execution model (Section 2.2 ) we provide an overview of the two types of conflict detection policies in STM (Section 2.3.1) that affects the execution pattern of tasks. We then present the Audsley's method (Section 3), which is a common technique to compute worst-case response time in the preemptive model, and show that this method cannot be directly applied to STM. A simple equation to compute WCRT in a STM system with 2 tasks is presented along with the concept of abort costs (Section 4). The transactional execution model of STM is transformed to a preemptive model by converting abort costs of tasks to phantom tasks. We then apply the Audsley's equation for determining WCRT for this enhanced task set, which gives us an approximate value of WCRT for the original task set (Section 5). Experimental results using task sets of various sizes are generated to evaluate the correctness of our approach (Section 6). We conclude with a review of related work (Section 7) and a reflection on our results (Section 8).

div.head: II. BASIC CONCEPTS AND EXECUTION MODEL
div.p: In this section, we introduce the basic concepts and the notation used to denote these concepts in the rest of the paper. In addition, we review the STM execution model and assumptions made in this study.

div.head: A. Basic Concepts
div.p: Essential concepts in STM are tasks and their associated priority, their associated time period and the dual concept of arrival rate, and their execution time; the concept of a time interval and release offset therein. div.head: B. Execution Model and Assumptions
div.p: We have considered an execution model of software transaction memory which runs on a uniprocessor system. Such a system is composed of independent threads, sharing a common memory based object such as a data structure or I/O buffer. Each thread is equivalent to a task, and every invocation of the thread involves a modification of the object. Each task is associated with a unique priority number, and the shared object is updated in consideration with task priorities (if two tasks are trying to access the object at the same time the higher priority task will update the object first). Each job of a task initiates a transaction which is said to have committed when it able to successfully change the shared object. If the transaction fails to commit, a new transaction is started by the task. The commit operation is performed at the end of the transaction and a job of a task is said to have completed when one if its transactions suc-cessfully commits. We assume a hard-real time system where every task has to complete execution strictly before its deadline elapses, otherwise the task set is deemed unschedulable.

When a transaction is initiated, a copy of the shared object is created and the transaction makes update to that object copy. The commit operation involves synchronizing the copy with the actual object. If a lower priority task was preempted and the shared object was changed by some other task, the copy of the shared object being used by the lower priority transaction becomes inconsistent, and the transaction has to be aborted and started again. The time to complete a transaction is same as the worst-case execution time of the task.

We assume that all jobs of tasks make changes to the same object. The method presented in this paper can easily be scaled to multiple shared objects by incrementing costs related to preemption. To cover all kinds of task sets, we consider the pessimistic case that when any higher priority task preempts a lower priority task, the transaction of the lower priority task will be aborted. A task set where preemption results in transaction restarts for only a few tasks is a sub-set of this pessimistic scenario. Also, while the execution time of a task will generally have a preemptive and transactional (when objects are being updated) execution phase, we keep the transaction and task execution times as same. Several sufficient schedulability tests exist for the preemptive model, hence determining schedulability for the preemptive phase is an unnecessary duplication of work.

By making such pessimistic assumptions we are able to focus only on the transactional phase of the execution, which is the model not understood well. Our method can be com-bined with tests for preemptive model to ascertain schedulability of a practical STM task set which will have both preemptive and transactional phases. There are also certain overheads associated with preemption and conflict detection policies which are generally only a fraction of the execution time of tasks. Analysis of even a simple transactional execution model is complex, hence in our current work, overheads associated with preemption and conflict detection policies have been ignored. We will enhance our method for consideration of such overheads in future work.

div.head: C. Lazy vs. Eager Conflict Detection
div.p: The conflict detection policy determines the point at which an inconsistency in the shared object is detected, thus allowing the lower priority to abort. For our STM model, in lazy conflict detection policy the task is assumed to execute for its WCET and then aborted, while in an eager conflict detection policy a conflict is detected as soon as it arises, allowing the job of a task to abort its transaction immediately without waiting for the commit stage. The execution semantics of these two policies are illustrated using an example in [5].

div.head: D. Critical Instance in STM
div.p: In response time studies for real-time systems, a critical instant of release is assumed. Unlike the preemptive model, in STM a synchronous release of tasks is not guaranteed to lead to WCRT with either conflict detection policy. The response time for W 1 in a synchronous release under lazy con- , where W 1 completes at time 15 in a synchronous release while the response time is 20 in the worst-case. Clearly, a synchronous release of tasks is not the guaranteed to lead to the worst-case in STM.
We now look at a sufficient and exact schedulability test widely used for analysis in the preemptive model.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY TEST FOR THE PREEMPTIVE MODEL

Since a synchronous release leads to the WCRT in the preemptive model, eq. (3.1) also computes the WCRT for a task. Hence, if this equation converges and the response time of some task W i * n is less than its deadline it means that W i is schedulable. By successively checking the response time of tasks W n-1 through W 1 present in a task set * n this way, the schedulability of * n can be sufficiently determined. If it is known that the system will have a synchronous release of tasks, this equation can also be used to build an exact schedulability test since in the preemptive model, no release scenario of higher priority tasks will give a higher response time than a synchronous release.

If this equation is applied to determine response time for W 1 in our example task set, it gives the response time for W 1 as 13. As seen in sections 2.3 and 2.4, the response time for W 1 with STM-LCD under synchronous release is 16, while in its worst-case release the response time is 27. For STM-ECD, the response times under synchronous and worst-case releases are 15 and 20 respectively. Clearly, Audsley's equation gives a lower value than the actual response time. If this method is used as a schedulability test for STM it will be satisfied even by unschedulable task sets, and thus fails to provide guaranteed results. For STM, Audsley's equation is restricted because it does not account for abort costs, as explained in the next section.

div.head: IV. SUFFICIENT TEST FOR 2-TASK SYSTEMS
div.p: In determining sufficient schedulability test, we first look at STM systems with 2 tasks. In this section, we show a theorem to determine WCRT in 2-task set using both STM-LCD and STM-ECD. Before that, we define the important concept of abort costs. Due to space constraint some proofs are provided in the expanded version of this paper [6].

div.head: A. Abort Costs
div.p: In our model of STM, a preempted task is aborted and restarted when no higher priority task is available for execution. The time spent in the aborted execution of a low priority task W j is not counted towards its execution hence, this time is considered as 'wasted' and therefore is an additional cost on the response time of W j . This additional cost is termed as the abort cost. In fig. 1(c), the abort costs induced on W 1 by W 2 and W 3 have been highlighted for STM-LCD, while the same have been highlighted in fig. 1(d) for STM-ECD. div.head: V. SUFFICIENT TESTS FOR n-TASK SYSTEMS
div.p: In STM systems with more than 2 tasks determining schedulability is complicated. An intuitive approach is to extend the sufficient schedulability results derived for 2-task sets to n-task sets. This can be done by releasing each higher priority task at times which induce maximum abort cost on a lower priority task. However, this is not guaranteed to lead to the WCRT.
Consider the following task set:

As per lemma 1, this release order induces abort costs of C 1 and C 2 on W 1 and W 2 respectively. In such a release scenario, W 1 completes at time 44.

However, in the worst-case release scenario W 1 completes at time 58 as shown in fig. 2(b). Note that in the worst-case release scenario the release of W 3 does not induce any abort cost on W 2 . Such a release scenario does not intuitively follow from the release scenario for 2-task system under STM-LCD.

Fig. 2(c) shows the execution of this task set in STM-ECD when tasks are released at the same time as in STM-LCD. As per lemma 2, such a release order induces the maximum abort costs of C 1 -1 and C 2 -1 that are possible on W 1 and W 2 , respectively. In this release scenario, W 1 completes at time 15. However, in the worst-case release scenario W 1 completes at time 20 as shown in fig. 2(d). In this worst-case release scenario, the first job of W 3 is released before the first job of W 2 . Such a release scenario also does not intuitively follow from the release scenario for 2-task systems under STM-ECD. We should point out that for our example task set (defined in section 2.3) the worst-case release scenario for STM-ECD follows the methodology given for 2-task sets (fig. 1(d)). The worst-case release scenarios under STM-LCD for both the examples is also different This clearly illustrates the fact that there is no specific release order that can deterministically lead to worst-case response time for all task sets. The only other technique is to compute the response time under an exponential order of combinations of possible release scenarios. The WCRT will be the highest among these response times and if this WCRT is less than the task deadline, the task set is guaranteed to be schedulable. Unfortunately, this approach is computationally expensive and scales exponentially with the size of the task set making its use impractical in most cases.

We now focus on a method that makes worst-case assumptions on abort costs and then determines the response time. We show how to add these worst-case abort costs to the task set and compute response time using Audsley's method described previously. A.

Abort Costs as Phantom Tasks Audsley's method is designed for preemptive execution and cannot characterize the abort costs that are found in STM. Therefore, to use this method we need to convert an STM model to a preemptive execution model. The abort costs induced on some task W j do not count as completed execution steps of W j . Hence, the processor time incurred on the execution of an aborted task can be considered as an independent task in itself. We call this a phantom task, and by characterizing abort costs this way a STM task set can be extended to a preemptive task set. The methodology of adding phantom tasks is guided by the following properties:
Property 1 [6]. Job of a higher priority task can induce abort costs to only a single job of one lower priority task.

Property 2 [6]. For STM-LCD, the maximum abort costs that can be induced by the release of a higher priority task W i , is C max , where C max is the maximum execution time among tasks of lower priority. Or,

div.p: When adding phantom tasks based on abort costs, the important task attributes that need to be ascertained is the execution time and arrival periods and the number of such tasks that need to be added. As shown previously, the abort costs induced on a task are not constant, and it is possible for higher priority tasks to be released without inducing any abort cost a lower priority task. However, since our scope is to determine a sufficient schedulability test, we can make pessimistic assumptions and over-approximate the abort costs that can be induced on lower priority tasks.

The goal of over-approximation allows us to assume that for each higher priority task there is an associated phantom task, whose execution time is equivalent to the maximum abort cost that can be induced by this higher priority task. The following points highlight our methodology of adding phantom tasks:

x The release of a job of some higher priority task W i creates a phantom task x The execution time of this phantom task is the maximum abort cost that W i can induce on lower priority tasks, defined by properties 2 and 3. x We associate each higher priority task with one phantom task and set the arrival period of the phantom task same that of the higher priority task. This insures that along with subsequent jobs of the higher priority task, the execution of the phantom task is also accounted for in calculations

When adding phantom tasks in such a pessimistic way we have to be cautious that the total utilization ratio of the new task set (original + phantom tasks) does not exceed 1. Liu and Layland [11] have shown that in this scenario the task set is not schedulable and in [3] Audsley et al show that their method will not converge when utilization exceeds 1. Hence, before adding a phantom task we need to check that the combined utilization ratio of the enhanced task set will be less than or equal to 1. If the combined utilization exceeds 1, it means that the task set will be unschedulable in the presence of worst-case abort costs and hence it fails the test.
Implementation details of our approach are provided in the next section.

div.head: B. Algorithm
div.p: The pseudo-code of the algorithm that adds phantom tasks to the original task set is given in table 1. For brevity, we have not provided details of the Audsley's method which has already been well illustrated. For a given task set * n and task index m, this algorithm provides a sufficient true/false value if the task W m and all tasks with higher priority than W m are schedulable under STM-LCD. The algorithm adds phantom tasks and computes the response time of task W m and all tasks having higher priority than W m . If the response time of W m or any task with higher priority is more than its deadline, then W m set is deemed unschedulable.

In the algorithm, the loop in lines 3-23 iterate to find the schedulability of higher priority tasks W n-1 through W m+1 as well as W m . The task whose schedulability is to be determined is identified by the index k. We compute the combined utilization ratios of tasks W k+1 through W n (line 8). The response time of W k is considered variable, hence the utilization ratio of W k cannot be determined. The loop in lines 9-19 iterates through each higher priority task starting with the one having highest priority. For each higher priority task W i we define attributes for a phantom task W p (lines 11-13). C p is the maximum abort cost that W i can induce on any lower priority task, while T p is same as T i . W p is added to * new (line 17) with these parameters only if the combined utilization ratio will not exceed 1. Otherwise the task set is deemed unschedulable and a false answer is returned (line 15). This way phantom tasks are added while maintaining the utilization bound.

We do not want to affect the execution semantics of the original task set. To achieve this, all phantom tasks are assigned priorities starting from k+1 and going higher, while priorities of tasks W k+1 to W n are re-assigned (line 20 -note that W k is still the lowest priority task in the set). Hence, phantom tasks have a higher priority than W k , but lower priority than task W k+1 in the original set * new .

Using phantom tasks, the transaction model has been converted to a preemptive execution model. We then apply Audsley's methods on the augmented task set * n to determine the response time of W k under a synchronous release, which is guaranteed to lead to the worst-case response time as proven in [11]. Note that as shown in Section 2.4, a synchronous release is not guaranteed to lead to the WCRT in STM. However, since we have converted the transactional model of STM to a preemptive model, results that have been derived for the preemptive model hold true for our expanded task set. Therefore, a synchronous release is guaranteed to lead to the worst case of our expanded task set.

This algorithm can easily be modified to sufficiently determine the schedulability of a task W k under STM-ECD as well. This can be done by modifying line 12 in the algorithm which sets the execution time of phantom tasks. Or, for STM-ECD line 12 is:

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS
div.p: We have analyzed the coverage of the sufficient schedulability test for STM using synthetic task sets. 7 groups of 500 task sets, were randomly generated. Task sets in the 1 st group had 2 tasks, 2 nd group has 3 tasks, and so on. 250 task sets in each group had total utilization ratio less than 0.5 while the other 250 has utilization ratios more than or equal to 0.5. These are sub-classified into the lower utilization and higher utilization categories respectively. All task sets were unique in the sense that at least one task was different between any two task sets. The arrival periods for the task sets were selected from the range [10,60] while their execution times were selected from [2,10]. These ranges were selected arbitrarily and kept low to reduce the time in analysis.

The % of schedulable task sets that satisfy the schedulability test for task sets of different sizes is plotted in figs. 3(a) -(d). None of the task sets which were unschedulable satisfied our schedulability test. In the lower utilization category, a higher % of tasks sets satisfy the sufficient tests for both STM-LCD (fig. 3(a)) and STM-ECD (fig. 3(c)). For STM-ECD the % does not change much with the increase in task set size. However, STM-LCD shows a marked drop in the cases showing that the degree of pessimism is much higher than STM-ECD for the same task set. For the higher utilization category, there is considerable drop in the percentage for both STM-LCD (fig. 3(b)) and STM-ECD (fig. 3(d)). The % also drops as the number of task sets increase, with the % for 8-task sets being as low as 2%. This decrease in the satisfiability for higher utilization group can be attributed to them reaching a combined utilization ratio greater than 1 when the worst-case abort costs are added as phantom tasks.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: Concurrency control has been a problem in the preemptive execution model, since it could affect schedulability of tasks and lead to the serious problem of priority inversion [19]. To avoid this, methods like Priority Ceiling protocol (PCP) [19] were proposed. Anderson et al [1] presented lock-free execution, one of the first transactional oriented models proposed for resolving concurrency control in real-time systems. In [1], response time analysis of lockfree execution under static and dynamic priority assignments have been presented. In [2], a linear programming approach to compute response time bounds in lock-free execution has been developed. However, we are not aware of any sufficient schedulability test that has been developed for this model.

Response time analysis models for multi-processor based STM systems have been proposed by Fahmy et al in [8], [9] as well as by Schoeberl et al [18] and Sarni et al [15]. In [8], a method for computing approximate values of WCRT in multi-processor scheduling has been presented. Since this method computes only an approximate value it cannot be used to derive schedulability tests which require guaranteed results. Sufficient schedulability tests which fo- if (RTk > Tk) return false 23. end loop k 24. return true cus on STM have not been presented yet. In [14], Mason et al develop a technique to implement atomic critical sections in Java and present basic response time analysis for this model. Basic comparisons of the temporal properties of lazy and eager conflict detection have been presented in [5].

A functional programming formalism has been proposed as another transaction based model for real-time systems. Called P-FRP [13], it requires a task to be executed atomically to maintain the state-less nature of program execution. Response time analysis for P-FRP has been presented by Belwal et al [4] and Kaiabachev et al [13].

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS AND ONGOING WORK
div.p: We have developed a sufficient schedulability test for Software Transactional memory, which works for both the lazy and eager conflict detection policies. Using phantom tasks, our method converts a transactional model to a pessimistic preemptive model and then uses the Audsley's method which is a common technique for computing response times and determining schedulability in the preemptive model. Evaluation using synthetic task sets shows that in STM-ECD several schedulable task sets satisfy our sufficient test, while the % satisfaction for STM-LCD is lower. The correctness of our tests was also validated in the evaluation, since no unschedulable task set satisfied the sufficient schedulability test.

The performance of our test is much better for task sets with lower utilization ratios since the lower utilization is able to accommodate the pessimistic assumptions made in our method. Even though task sets with higher utilization cannot accommodate the worst-case preemption costs they can still be schedulable if a release scenario which can induce worstcase costs cannot exist. In future work, we will be developing techniques to lower the pessimism in the process of creating phantom tasks.
